en.title: Botany: the whole course
en.short: What botany covers, how botany degrees are organised, and how to study the subject well.

sections.heading: What botany is
sections.text:
Botany is the scientific study of plants: their structure, function, growth, reproduction, diversity, evolution, ecology and uses. It asks how a plant survives in its habitat, how it is built, how it makes food, how it reproduces, and how it relates to other organisms. Many botany courses also study algae, fungi and lichens. Modern classification places fungi outside the plant kingdom, but they are often taught in botany because of their traditional place in plant science and their importance in agriculture and ecology.

Botany matters for food, medicine, forestry, conservation and climate science. These summaries teach principles and standard methods. They do not replace laboratory work, field observation, your local flora or your department’s safety rules. Names of species and classifications change, so check current sources.

sections.heading: How a degree is organised
sections.text:
Degree length and awards differ by country and institution, so check your handbook. In Nigeria, a BSc in Botany, Plant Science or Plant Biology is commonly a four-year degree, and some programmes include supervised industrial work experience under SIWES. In the UK, a BSc is usually three years in England, Wales and Northern Ireland and four in Scotland; an integrated master’s usually adds a year. In the United States, a bachelor’s degree is usually four years. A master’s degree commonly takes one or two years and ends with a dissertation.

Early years usually share biology, chemistry, mathematics and statistics with other life-science students. Later years add plant-specific subjects, laboratory and field work, and often a final-year project. Master’s courses add advanced theory, research methods and a supervised dissertation.

sections.heading: The main areas, in teaching order
sections.text:
The introductory stage builds the tools. You begin with the scientific method, microscopy and botanical measurement, then statistics and experimental design. Next come plant cell structure, tissues and meristems, the regions where growth occurs, vegetative morphology of roots, stems and leaves, and reproductive morphology of flowers, fruits and seeds. Classification and nomenclature, the rules of naming, introduce plant names. Plant diversity and life cycles show how major groups reproduce. Water relations and transport, and photosynthesis and respiration, introduce plant function.

The core stage deepens anatomy and secondary growth, then systematics, the study of relationships and classification, and herbarium practice, the care of pressed, labelled specimens. You study algae, fungi and lichens, bryophytes and pteridophytes, and gymnosperms and angiosperm diversity. Water relations and mineral nutrition, carbon metabolism, hormones and development follow. Genetics and breeding, molecular biology and biotechnology connect plants to modern science. Ecology covers populations, communities and ecosystems. Plant pathology and pest management deal with disease and crop loss. Economic botany and ethnobotany cover uses and local knowledge. Conservation biology, field methods, research projects and professional ethics complete the core.

At master’s level, typical topics are advanced plant genomics and bioinformatics, plant biotechnology and genetic engineering, advanced plant ecology and climate change, and research methods leading to a dissertation.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Study with real plants. Learn terms beside a specimen, a microscope slide or a diagram. Draw labelled diagrams from memory, then check them. For life cycles, draw the alternation of generations, the cycle between the gametophyte stage, which makes gametes, and the sporophyte stage, which makes spores. Mark where meiosis, the division that halves chromosome number, and fertilisation occur. Link every structure to a function and every function to the plant’s habitat.

Keep a field notebook and, where your course requires it, a herbarium of pressed specimens with full collection data. Practise microscope technique and record magnification and scale bars. Work through statistics and physiology calculations by hand. Read the sources your lecturers give, and use current plant guides and nomenclature databases. Follow laboratory and field safety rules, and record data honestly.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
Common mistakes include memorising names without understanding function, and copying diagrams without labels or scale. Students confuse the gametophyte and sporophyte stages, or forget that meiosis and fertilisation occur at different points in different groups. Others treat common names as scientific names, assume all fungi are plants, or ignore updated classification.

In microscopy, students forget units, magnification or scale bars. In ecology and physiology, they take one specimen or one reading as a general rule. Poor field notes make later identification impossible. In projects, students leave collecting, identification and writing too late. Start early, keep records, and ask for help with identification and statistics.

keyPoints: Botany is the scientific study of plants, including their structure, function, diversity, ecology and uses.
Degree length and awards vary by country and institution, so check your handbook.
Learn plant structure and life cycles with specimens, labelled diagrams and clear comparisons.
Fungi are not plants in modern classification, though many botany courses still teach them.
Record field and laboratory work carefully, with units, dates, locations and scale.
Field safety, honest data and professional ethics are part of botanical training.

en.title: Scientific method, microscopy and botanical measurement
en.short: Hypothesis and variables, light and dissecting microscopes, slides, drawing, units, accuracy and safety.

sections.heading: Scientific method
sections.text: Science works by observation, questions, hypotheses and tests. A hypothesis is a testable statement that evidence can support or reject. In an experiment, the independent variable is what you change, the dependent variable is what you measure, and controlled variables are kept constant so they do not confuse the result. A control group receives no treatment or a standard treatment. Record raw data at the time. A hypothesis is never proved for ever; it is supported or rejected by evidence.

sections.heading: Microscopes and slides
sections.text: A compound light microscope uses an eyepiece and objective lenses to magnify thin, translucent material. Total magnification = eyepiece magnification × objective magnification. A dissecting microscope has lower magnification and a longer working distance, so it is used for whole flowers, insects or leaves. Resolution is the smallest separation that can be seen; magnification beyond the resolution gives an empty, blurred image. Make a temporary slide by placing a thin specimen in a drop of water or stain, then lowering a coverslip at an angle to avoid air bubbles. Iodine solution makes starch visible; other stains mark particular cell parts. Handle slides by the edges.

sections.heading: Drawing, measurement, safety
sections.text: Botanical drawings record shape and arrangement. Use a sharp pencil, draw large, keep outlines clear, avoid shading, and label with straight lines that do not cross. SI units: 1 cm = 10 mm and 1 mm = 1,000 micrometres. Magnification = image size ÷ actual size. Example: a 2.5 mm structure is drawn 50 mm long, so magnification = 50 ÷ 2.5 = ×20. If a drawing at ×20 shows a part 30 mm long, actual size = 30 ÷ 20 = 1.5 mm. Accuracy means closeness to the true value; precision means repeated readings agree. Use a calibrated eyepiece scale or a stage micrometer, a slide with a known scale, for microscope measurement. Safety: wear goggles and a lab coat, handle blades and glass carefully, carry microscopes upright, and report spills at once.

keyPoints: A hypothesis is a testable statement; experiments change one independent variable and measure one dependent variable.
Total microscope magnification = eyepiece magnification × objective magnification.
Resolution limits useful magnification; a blurred image cannot be improved by magnifying more.
Make temporary slides with a thin specimen, water or stain, and a coverslip lowered at an angle.
Magnification = image size ÷ actual size; 1 mm = 1,000 micrometres.
Accuracy is closeness to the true value; precision is agreement between repeats; follow laboratory safety rules.

en.title: Botanical statistics and experimental design
en.short: Data types, sampling, descriptive statistics, probability, hypothesis tests and simple designs.

sections.heading: Data and sampling
sections.text: Data are categorical when they name groups, such as flower colour, and quantitative when they are numbers, such as leaf length or seed count. Quantitative data may be discrete counts or continuous measurements. Define the population, then take a sample. Random sampling gives every unit an equal chance and reduces bias. Systematic sampling takes every kth unit after a random start; stratified sampling divides the population into strata such as soil types and samples within each. Report the sample size and method: a large biased sample is misleading.

sections.heading: Describing and testing
sections.text: For n observations, mean = Σx ÷ n; median is the middle ordered value or the mean of the two middle values. Mode is the most frequent. Sample variance = Σ(x − mean)² ÷ (n − 1); SD = √variance. SD measures spread among observations; SE = SD ÷ √n measures uncertainty in a mean. Example: lengths 4.2, 4.6, 4.8, 5.0, 5.4 cm. Mean = 24.0 ÷ 5 = 4.8 cm. Σ(x − mean)² = 0.80, variance = 0.80 ÷ 4 = 0.20 cm², SD = 0.45 cm, SE = 0.45 ÷ √5 = 0.20 cm. Probability ranges from 0 to 1. In a hypothesis test, state a null hypothesis (no difference) and an alternative. Choose a significance level α, commonly 0.05. A p-value is the probability of data at least as extreme as observed if the null is true; it is not the probability that the null is true. Reject the null if p < α.

sections.heading: Experimental design
sections.text: Replication means independent units receive the same treatment; repeated measurements on one plant are pseudoreplication. Randomisation assigns treatments or samples by chance, so unseen differences do not favour one treatment. Include controls. A completely randomised design assigns treatments randomly to all units. A randomised complete block design groups units into blocks of similar conditions, such as bench position, then randomises treatments within each block. A factorial design tests two or more factors and their interaction, meaning the effect of one factor depends on the other, for example fertiliser rate and watering frequency.

keyPoints: Categorical data name groups; quantitative data are counted or measured.
Mean = Σx ÷ n; sample SD = √(Σ(x − mean)² ÷ (n − 1)); SE = SD ÷ √n.
A p-value is the chance of data at least as extreme as observed if the null hypothesis is true.
Replication uses independent experimental units; repeated measurements on one plant are pseudoreplication.
Randomisation assigns treatments or samples by chance to avoid bias.
Completely randomised, randomised complete block and factorial designs are common in botany.

en.title: Plant cell structure and organelles
en.short: Plant cell walls, membranes, vacuoles, plastids, nucleus, organelles, plasmodesmata and plant-animal differences.

sections.heading: Cell wall and membrane
sections.text: Plant cells are eukaryotic: their DNA is enclosed in a nucleus. Outside the plasma membrane is a cell wall, mainly cellulose microfibrils in a matrix of pectin and hemicellulose. It gives shape, strength and protection. The plasma membrane is a phospholipid bilayer with proteins; it is selectively permeable, controlling what enters and leaves. A thin onion epidermal peel can show the wall and a large vacuole clearly under a light microscope.

sections.heading: Vacuole and plastids
sections.text: The vacuole is a large sac bounded by the tonoplast. Its cell sap stores water, ions, sugars and pigments, and its pressure helps keep young cells firm, a state called turgor. Plastids are a group of organelles found in plants. Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll and carry out photosynthesis; chromoplasts store coloured pigments; leucoplasts store starch or oils. Mitochondria release energy from sugars.

sections.heading: Nucleus and organelles
sections.text: The nucleus holds chromatin, made of DNA and protein, and a nucleolus, where ribosomes are assembled. A double nuclear envelope with pores controls traffic to the cytoplasm. Other organelles include the endoplasmic reticulum, a membrane network for making and moving proteins and lipids; the Golgi apparatus, which modifies and packages materials; ribosomes, the sites of protein synthesis; and peroxisomes, which handle some metabolic reactions.

sections.heading: Connections and differences
sections.text: Plasmodesmata are narrow channels through the cell wall that connect the cytoplasm of neighbouring cells, forming the symplast. The cytoskeleton is a network of microtubules and actin microfilaments; it supports the cell, guides organelle movement and helps form the cell plate during division. Plant and animal cells share a nucleus, plasma membrane, mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi and ribosomes. Plant cells also have a wall, plastids, a large central vacuole and plasmodesmata. Animal cells have no cell wall or plastids and usually only small vacuoles.

keyPoints: Plant cells have a cellulose cell wall outside the selectively permeable plasma membrane.
The large vacuole, bounded by the tonoplast, stores cell sap and maintains turgor.
Plastids include chloroplasts for photosynthesis, chromoplasts for pigments and leucoplasts for storage.
The nucleus contains chromatin and a nucleolus and is bounded by a nuclear envelope with pores.
Plasmodesmata connect neighbouring cells through the wall, and the cytoskeleton supports and guides the cell.
Unlike animal cells, plant cells have a wall, plastids, a large central vacuole and plasmodesmata.

en.title: Plant tissues and meristems
en.short: Meristems, simple and complex tissues, xylem and phloem, and primary versus secondary growth.

sections.heading: Meristems
sections.text: Meristems are regions of small, dividing cells. Their cells are small, with thin walls and dense cytoplasm. Apical meristems sit at root and shoot tips and produce primary growth, which lengthens the plant. Lateral meristems, such as the vascular cambium and cork cambium, run as cylinders inside stems and roots; they produce secondary growth, which increases girth. Most monocots lack a vascular cambium, so they usually do not thicken in this way; many dicots and gymnosperms do.

sections.heading: Simple tissues
sections.text: Parenchyma cells are living, thin-walled and unspecialised. They store starch, photosynthesise in leaves and help repair wounds. Collenchyma cells are living with unevenly thickened walls; they give flexible support to young stems and petioles. Sclerenchyma cells have thick walls strengthened with lignin and are dead at maturity. Fibres and sclereids are sclerenchyma and strengthen mature plant parts.

sections.heading: Tissue systems
sections.text: The dermal tissue system is the outer covering: epidermis in young plants and periderm, a corky layer, in older ones. Ground tissue fills the space between dermal and vascular tissues; it is mostly parenchyma, with some collenchyma and sclerenchyma. Vascular tissue contains xylem and phloem. Xylem carries water and minerals upward and has dead conducting cells called tracheids and vessel elements. Phloem carries sugars and other substances; its sieve tube elements are living and are helped by companion cells.

sections.heading: Growth in a stem
sections.text: Primary growth comes from apical meristems and secondary growth from lateral meristems. Case: a young sunflower stem first lengthens by its apical meristem. Later its vascular cambium divides, adding xylem to the inside and phloem to the outside, so the stem thickens. The outer epidermis may be replaced by cork as the stem ages. The exact pattern varies between species.

keyPoints: Apical meristems at root and shoot tips give primary growth; lateral meristems give secondary growth.
Parenchyma is living and thin-walled; collenchyma is living with uneven walls; sclerenchyma is dead with lignified walls.
Dermal tissue covers the plant; ground tissue fills the body; vascular tissue contains xylem and phloem.
Xylem carries water upward through dead tracheids and vessel elements; phloem carries sugars through living sieve tubes and companion cells.
Most monocots lack a vascular cambium, so they usually do not thicken by secondary growth.

en.title: Vegetative morphology: roots, stems and leaves
en.short: Root systems, stem forms, leaf parts, phyllotaxy, venation and common vegetative modifications.

sections.heading: Root systems
sections.text: Roots anchor the plant, absorb water and minerals, and may store food. A taproot system develops from the radicle, the first root of the seedling, and has one main root with lateral roots. A fibrous root system has many similar roots and no dominant main root; it is common in grasses. Root hairs are fine extensions of epidermal cells that increase absorption. Adventitious roots arise from stems or leaves.

sections.heading: Stems and forms
sections.text: The stem supports leaves and flowers and conducts water and food. It bears nodes, where leaves attach, and internodes between them. Stems may be herbaceous (soft) or woody (hardened with secondary growth). Aerial forms include erect, climbing, creeping and trailing stems. Underground stems include rhizomes, tubers and corms; they are stems because they have nodes, buds or scale leaves.

sections.heading: Leaves and arrangement
sections.text: A typical leaf has a blade or lamina, a petiole (stalk), and sometimes stipules at the base. The midrib and veins form the vascular framework. Phyllotaxy is the arrangement of leaves on the stem: alternate (one per node), opposite (two per node) and whorled (three or more per node). Venation is the pattern of veins: reticulate (net-like, common in dicotyledons) or parallel (common in monocotyledons); reticulate may be pinnate or palmate.

sections.heading: Modifications
sections.text: Vegetative modifications are altered roots, stems or leaves with special functions. Storage roots include cassava and carrot. Prop roots of maize support the stem; buttress roots of some tropical trees support large trunks; pneumatophores in mangroves help roots obtain air. Stem modifications include rhizomes for spread and storage, tubers such as potato for storage, stolons for propagation, tendrils for climbing and thorns for protection. Leaf modifications include tendrils for climbing, spines for protection, fleshy scales for storage and phyllodes for reduced water loss.

keyPoints: A taproot system has one main root; a fibrous system has many similar roots.
Stems bear nodes and internodes and may be herbaceous or woody.
A typical leaf has a blade, a petiole and sometimes stipules.
Phyllotaxy is alternate, opposite or whorled; venation is reticulate or parallel.
Vegetative modifications are roots, stems or leaves altered for storage, support, climbing, protection or reduced water loss.
Examples include cassava storage roots, maize prop roots, potato tubers and leaf tendrils.

en.title: Reproductive morphology: flowers, fruits and seeds
en.short: Flower parts, symmetry, ovary position, inflorescences, fruit and seed types, floral formulae and diagrams.

sections.heading: Flower parts and symmetry
sections.text: A flower is a shortened shoot bearing modified leaves. The sterile whorls are the calyx (sepals) and corolla (petals), together the perianth. The fertile whorls are the androecium (stamens, each with anther and filament) and gynoecium (carpels, each with stigma, style and ovary). Symmetry is actinomorphic when the flower can be divided into similar halves in several planes, and zygomorphic when only one plane gives mirror halves. The ovary is superior when the other parts attach below it, and inferior when they attach above it.

sections.heading: Inflorescences
sections.text: An inflorescence is a group of flowers on one branch system. In racemose (indeterminate) types the main axis keeps growing and the lower or outer flowers open first; examples are the raceme, spike, umbel and capitulum. In cymose (determinate) types the main axis ends in a flower and side branches continue the cluster; a cyme is the basic form. A capitulum, the flower head of Asteraceae such as sunflower, is a racemose inflorescence.

sections.heading: Fruits and seeds
sections.text: A fruit develops from the ovary after fertilisation and protects and disperses seeds. Simple fruits come from one ovary: a legume, capsule, berry or drupe. Aggregate fruits come from many separate carpels of one flower, as in raspberry. Multiple fruits come from several flowers, as in pineapple. Dry fruits may dehisce (split open) or remain indehiscent. A seed contains an embryo, food in endosperm or cotyledons, and a testa (seed coat). Example: a cowpea pod is a legume, a dry dehiscent fruit; its seeds have two cotyledons storing the food.

sections.heading: Floral formulae and diagrams
sections.text: A floral formula uses K, C, A and G for calyx, corolla, androecium and gynoecium. Numbers show part counts; parentheses show fusion; a bar above G marks an inferior ovary. For example, the pea flower (Fabaceae) is zygomorphic: K(5) C5 A(9)+1 G1. A floral diagram is a cross-section: sepals outermost, then petals, stamens, and carpels at the centre; fusion and ovary position are drawn. Check your course’s conventions.

keyPoints: A flower has sterile whorls (calyx, corolla) and fertile whorls (androecium, gynoecium).
Actinomorphic flowers are radially symmetric; zygomorphic flowers are bilaterally symmetric.
The ovary is superior when other parts attach below it and inferior when they attach above it.
Inflorescences are racemose (indeterminate) or cymose (determinate); a capitulum is a flower head.
Fruits are simple, aggregate or multiple, and may be dry or fleshy, dehiscent or indehiscent.
A floral formula uses K, C, A, G, numbers, parentheses and ovary bars; a floral diagram is a cross-section.

en.title: Plant classification and nomenclature
en.short: Taxonomic hierarchy, binomial names, type specimens, the ICN and simple dichotomous keys.
keywords: International Code of Nomenclature for algae, fungi, and plants

sections.heading: Taxonomic hierarchy
sections.text: Classification groups organisms by shared features and, ideally, by common ancestry. Taxonomists arrange groups in a hierarchy of ranks: kingdom, division (phylum), class, order, family, genus and species. Each rank contains one or more groups of the rank below. Ranks are conventions, not fixed natural units. Family names under the botanical Code usually end in -aceae and order names in -ales. Example: maize is Zea mays in the grass family Poaceae.

sections.heading: Binomial names
sections.text: Binomial nomenclature gives every species a two-part Latinised name. The first part is the genus, written with a capital letter; the second is the specific epithet, written in lower case. Both are italicised in print or underlined by hand. The author citation may follow: Zea mays L., where L. is the standard abbreviation for Linnaeus. After first mention the genus may be shortened, as Z. mays. A name is a label, not a description, and it is governed by rules.

sections.heading: Type specimens and the Code
sections.text: The International Code of Nomenclature for algae, fungi, and plants (ICN) sets the rules for naming plants, algae and fungi. It is updated by International Botanical Congresses; check the current edition. A name is tied to a type specimen, usually a dried herbarium specimen deposited in a recognised collection. The holotype is the single specimen designated by the author. Isotypes are duplicates from the same gathering. The type need not look typical; it fixes the application of the name.

sections.heading: Identification keys
sections.text:
A dichotomous key identifies a specimen by a series of choices between two contrasting statements, called a couplet. Each statement is a lead, numbered 1a and 1b. Use clear, observable characters and check several specimens. Simple key to three crops:
1a Leaves long, narrow, parallel-veined; plant a grass: maize (Zea mays)
1b Leaves broader, net-veined: go to 2
2a Leaves palmately lobed: cassava (Manihot esculenta)
2b Leaves pinnately compound with four leaflets: groundnut (Arachis hypogaea)

keyPoints: Taxonomic ranks run kingdom, division, class, order, family, genus, species.
A binomial is genus plus specific epithet, italicised, with author citation optional.
A type specimen permanently anchors the application of a scientific name.
The ICN is the rulebook for names of algae, fungi and plants; check its current edition.
A dichotomous key uses paired leads and observable characters.
Classification should reflect shared ancestry where evidence allows, but ranks are human conventions.

en.title: Plant diversity and life cycles
en.short: Major plant groups, alternation of generations, heterospory and the seed habit.

sections.heading: Major plant groups
sections.text: Algae are a loose grouping of photosynthetic organisms, not one evolutionary line. Green algae are the closest relatives of land plants. Bryophytes (mosses, liverworts, hornworts) are small non-vascular plants: they lack true roots, stems and leaves, and need water for sperm to swim. Pteridophytes (ferns and allies) have vascular tissue, which conducts water and food, and reproduce by spores. Gymnosperms, such as conifers, bear seeds not enclosed in an ovary (seed case). Angiosperms are flowering plants; their seeds are enclosed in a fruit.

sections.heading: Alternation of generations
sections.text: All land plants show alternation of generations: a haploid gametophyte (n, one set of chromosomes) makes gametes (sex cells) by mitosis (ordinary cell division), and a diploid sporophyte (2n, two sets) makes spores (single cells that grow into a gametophyte) by meiosis (division that halves the chromosome number). The two stages differ in size and independence. In bryophytes the green leafy plant is the gametophyte and the sporophyte is a stalk and capsule dependent on it. In pteridophytes the sporophyte is the familiar fern and the gametophyte is a small separate plant. In seed plants the sporophyte dominates and the gametophytes are microscopic and dependent.

sections.heading: Heterospory and seeds
sections.text: Heterospory is the production of two spore types: microspores, which form male gametophytes, and megaspores, which form female gametophytes. It arose in some pteridophytes and is general in seed plants. The seed habit follows: the megaspore stays inside the parent sporophyte, the female gametophyte and embryo develop there, and a seed coat protects them. A seed therefore contains an embryo, stored food and a coat. The stored food gives the embryo a better start than a single-celled spore can get.

sections.heading: A moss example
sections.text: In a moss such as Funaria, rain lets sperm swim from the male gametophyte to the egg. The fertilised egg, or zygote, grows into the dependent sporophyte, which releases spores. Each spore can grow into a new gametophyte. This dependence on water is why bryophytes are common in damp habitats.

keyPoints: Algae are a loose grouping, and green algae are the closest relatives of land plants.
Alternation of generations alternates a haploid gametophyte with a diploid sporophyte.
Bryophytes have a dominant gametophyte and a dependent sporophyte; pteridophytes have a dominant sporophyte.
Seed plants have microscopic, dependent gametophytes.
Heterospory means producing microspores and megaspores.
The seed habit keeps the megaspore and embryo inside the parent and adds a protective coat.

en.title: Plant water relations and transport
en.short: Water potential, osmosis, root absorption, transpiration, xylem cohesion-tension and phloem translocation.

sections.heading: Water potential and osmosis
sections.text:
Water potential (Ψ) is the free energy of water per unit volume relative to pure water at the same temperature and pressure (0 MPa). It is the sum of solute potential (Ψs, negative) and pressure potential (Ψp, positive in turgid cells, negative in xylem). Water moves from higher (less negative) to lower (more negative) Ψ.

Osmosis is water diffusion across a selectively permeable membrane down a water potential gradient. Example: Ψs = −0.5 MPa and Ψp = +0.3 MPa give Ψ = −0.2 MPa. If the outside solution is −0.1 MPa, water enters the cell (−0.1 > −0.2).

sections.heading: Absorption and transpiration
sections.text:
Root hairs absorb most water because they greatly increase surface area. Water crosses the cortex through cell walls (apoplast) and cytoplasm (symplast) before entering xylem.

Transpiration is evaporation from leaf surfaces through stomata; it pulls water up and cools leaves. Stomata open for carbon dioxide but lose water. Case: tomato seedlings wilt at midday when transpiration exceeds root absorption, then recover by evening.

sections.heading: Xylem cohesion-tension
sections.text:
Cohesion-tension theory explains how water rises in xylem, the water-conducting tissue. Evaporation from mesophyll cell walls creates tension (negative pressure) in the xylem. Water molecules cohere by hydrogen bonds and adhere to xylem walls, so the column is pulled upward without breaking.

If air enters (cavitation), the column breaks; plants may refill vessels or use alternative pathways. Xylem transport is mainly upward and passive, driven by transpiration.

sections.heading: Phloem translocation
sections.text:
Translocation is the movement of sugars and other solutes in phloem, the sugar-conducting tissue, from source (where sugars are made or released from storage) to sink (where used or stored). The pressure-flow hypothesis: sucrose is actively loaded into sieve tubes at the source, lowering water potential; water enters by osmosis, raising pressure. At the sink, sucrose is unloaded, water leaves, and pressure falls.

Sap flows from high to low pressure. Phloem transport is bidirectional between sources and sinks and needs energy for loading.

keyPoints: Water potential: Ψ = Ψs + Ψp; pure water at standard conditions is 0 MPa.
Water moves from higher (less negative) to lower (more negative) water potential; osmosis is this movement across a selectively permeable membrane.
Root hairs absorb most water; transpiration through stomata creates the pull that drives xylem transport.
Cohesion-tension: transpiration creates negative pressure, and cohesion plus adhesion keep the water column continuous.
Phloem translocation follows the pressure-flow hypothesis: active loading at the source and unloading at the sink drive bulk flow.
Xylem transport is mainly upward and passive; phloem transport is bidirectional between sources and sinks and needs energy for loading.

en.title: Photosynthesis and respiration in plants
en.short: Light reactions, Calvin cycle, photorespiration, C4 and CAM; plant glycolysis, Krebs cycle and electron transport.

sections.heading: Light reactions
sections.text: In the thylakoid membranes, photosystem II splits water, releasing oxygen, electrons and protons. Light drives electrons through an electron transport chain. The chain pumps protons into the thylakoid lumen, and ATP synthase uses the proton gradient to make ATP. Photosystem I reduces NADP+ to NADPH. The main products are ATP and NADPH, which carry energy and reducing power to the stroma. Cyclic electron flow makes ATP but no NADPH.

sections.heading: Carbon fixation
sections.text: The Calvin cycle in the stroma fixes CO2. Rubisco joins CO2 to ribulose 1,5-bisphosphate (RuBP), forming 3-phosphoglycerate (3-PGA). ATP and NADPH reduce 3-PGA to glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate (G3P), and most G3P regenerates RuBP. Rubisco can also bind O2, starting photorespiration, which consumes ATP and releases CO2. C4 plants fix CO2 first in mesophyll cells with phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP) carboxylase, then run the Calvin cycle in bundle-sheath cells. CAM plants fix CO2 at night and run the Calvin cycle by day. Both reduce photorespiration and water loss.

sections.heading: Respiration
sections.text: Glycolysis in the cytosol converts glucose to pyruvate, with a net gain of 2 ATP and 2 NADH per glucose. Pyruvate is oxidised to acetyl-CoA, releasing CO2 and making NADH. The Krebs cycle in the mitochondrial matrix oxidises acetyl-CoA, releasing CO2 and making NADH, FADH2 and some ATP. The electron transport chain on the inner mitochondrial membrane passes electrons to oxygen and pumps protons. ATP synthase makes most of the ATP. Plant mitochondria also have alternative oxidase, so ATP yield varies.

sections.heading: Carbon balance
sections.text: Net carbon gain is gross photosynthesis minus respiration. Example: if a leaf fixes 12 micromol CO2 per square metre per second and respires 2, net uptake is 12 − 2 = 10 micromol CO2 per square metre per second. At night, gross photosynthesis is zero, so the leaf loses carbon. The same equation applies to crop canopies.

keyPoints: Light reactions split water, release O2 and make ATP and NADPH.
The Calvin cycle uses ATP and NADPH to fix CO2 through rubisco.
Photorespiration wastes carbon; C4 and CAM reduce it by separating CO2 fixation in space or time.
Glycolysis nets 2 ATP and 2 NADH per glucose.
The Krebs cycle and electron transport chain make most ATP, but exact yields vary.
Net CO2 uptake = gross photosynthesis − respiration.

en.title: Plant anatomy and secondary growth
en.short: Primary root, stem and leaf anatomy, cambia, wood, periderm and environmental adaptations.

sections.heading: Primary body
sections.text:
Primary tissues from apical meristems make up the young plant. In a root, epidermis absorbs water and bears root hairs; cortex stores food; the endodermis, with a waxy Casparian strip, controls entry to the stele; pericycle surrounds the vascular tissue. Dicot roots usually have a central star of xylem; monocot roots often have pith.

A dicot stem has epidermis, cortex, a ring of vascular bundles and pith. Each bundle has xylem and phloem separated by cambium. Monocot stems have scattered bundles. A leaf has epidermis with cuticle and stomata, mesophyll, and veins with bundle sheaths.

sections.heading: Cambia
sections.text: Secondary growth comes from two lateral meristems. Vascular cambium is a cylinder of dividing cells. It produces secondary xylem inward and secondary phloem outward, widening the stem or root. In dicot stems it first lies inside bundles and later joins into a ring. Cork cambium, or phellogen, forms in outer tissues. It produces cork (phellem) outward and phelloderm inward. Cork cells die and become suberised, a waterproof layer. Periderm means phellem, phellogen and phelloderm. Lenticels are loose patches for gas exchange.

sections.heading: Wood and bark
sections.text: Wood is secondary xylem. Earlywood forms in fast growth: wide vessels, thin walls. Latewood forms later: narrower cells, thicker walls. In many temperate trees this makes an annual ring; tropical species may lack clear rings. Heartwood is darker and no longer conducts water; sapwood conducts. Bark is all tissue outside the vascular cambium, including secondary phloem and periderm.

sections.heading: Environmental anatomy
sections.text:
Anatomy changes with habitat. Xerophyte leaves often have thick cuticles, sunken stomata, hairs and water-storage tissue. Hydrophytes have aerenchyma, large air spaces, thin cuticles and little supporting xylem. Halophytes may have salt glands and succulent leaves.

Case: Ngozi compares a maize stem and a mango twig. Maize has scattered bundles and no vascular cambium, so it makes no true wood. Mango has a bundle ring and cambium, so it adds wood and periderm.

keyPoints: Primary root, stem and leaf anatomy differ in the arrangement of epidermis, cortex, vascular tissue and pith.
Vascular cambium produces secondary xylem inward and secondary phloem outward.
Cork cambium produces cork outward and phelloderm inward; periderm is the three layers together.
Wood is secondary xylem; earlywood and latewood can form annual rings in some species, but not all.
Xerophytes show thick cuticles, sunken stomata and water storage; hydrophytes show aerenchyma and thin cuticles.
Monocots usually lack a vascular cambium, so they do not form true secondary wood; dicots and gymnosperms usually do.

en.title: Plant systematics and herbarium practice
en.short: Species concepts, cladistics and molecular phylogeny, keys, herbarium data, nomenclature and revision.

sections.heading: Species concepts
sections.text: A species concept is a rule for deciding whether populations belong to one species. The biological concept, associated with Ernst Mayr, treats species as interbreeding groups reproductively isolated from others. It fails for asexual plants, many hybrids and fossils. The morphological concept groups by consistent form, which is practical in herbaria but can hide cryptic species. Phylogenetic and evolutionary concepts use ancestry and separate lineages. Botanists often combine concepts and state which they use.

sections.heading: Cladistics and molecules
sections.text: Cladistics groups taxa by shared derived characters, called synapomorphies, and seeks monophyletic groups: an ancestor and all its descendants. Paraphyletic groups omit descendants; polyphyletic groups mix unrelated lineages. An outgroup helps polarise character states. Molecular phylogeny compares aligned DNA sequences, often plastid and nuclear regions, under an evolutionary model. Parsimony, likelihood and Bayesian methods build trees, and bootstrap or posterior probabilities show support. Trees are hypotheses; gene trees can differ from species trees.

sections.heading: Keys and specimens
sections.text: An identification key is a set of choices, usually dichotomous, where each couplet offers two leads. Good keys use clear, contrasting characters. Check both leads and confirm the result against a full description and specimen. A herbarium specimen is a pressed, dried plant with a label giving collector, collection number, date, locality, coordinates, habitat and notes. Herbaria hold type specimens, the permanent reference for names, and their data support distribution and conservation studies. Collect only with permission.

sections.heading: Nomenclature and revision
sections.text: Plant nomenclature follows the International Code of Nomenclature for algae, fungi, and plants. A name is validly published only if it meets the Code: effective publication, a description or diagnosis, and a type. Priority decides between competing names. A taxonomic revision tests names against specimens and types, then publishes a key, descriptions, synonymy and distribution. If two names prove to be the same species, the earlier valid name is kept and the later becomes a synonym. Revision stabilises names but remains a hypothesis.

keyPoints: Species concepts include biological, morphological, phylogenetic and evolutionary views, each with limits.
Cladistics recognises monophyletic groups by shared derived characters called synapomorphies.
Molecular phylogenies are hypotheses built from aligned DNA under an evolutionary model, with branch support.
Dichotomous keys use paired leads and must be checked against descriptions and specimens.
Herbarium labels should record collector, number, date, locality, coordinates and habitat, and type specimens fix names.
Under the ICN, valid publication, priority and typification govern names, and revisions publish keys, descriptions and synonymy.

en.title: Algae, fungi and lichens
en.short: Morphology, reproduction, ecology and uses of algae, fungi and lichens, including lichen symbiosis.

sections.heading: Form and groups
sections.text: Algae are photosynthetic organisms that are not a single evolutionary group. They range from unicellular phytoplankton to filaments, colonies and large seaweeds. Cyanobacteria are often called blue-green algae but are bacteria. Fungi are heterotrophs with chitinous cell walls and absorptive nutrition. They grow as yeasts, moulds or mushrooms. A mycelium is a network of hyphae, the thread-like filaments that make up the fungus body. Lichens are composite structures, not single organisms.

sections.heading: Reproduction
sections.text: Algae reproduce asexually by fragmentation, cell division or spores, and sexually by gametes. Many have life cycles that alternate haploid and diploid stages. Fungi reproduce by spores, both asexually and sexually; a single mushroom can release many spores. Lichens spread mainly by fragments, soredia (powdery packets of fungus and photobiont) and isidia (small outgrowths). The fungus usually reproduces sexually, but the partnership itself is not sexually reproduced.

sections.heading: Ecology and uses
sections.text: Algae are major aquatic primary producers and phytoplankton form the base of many food webs. They also cause harmful blooms when nutrients are excessive. Fungi are key decomposers and saprotrophs, organisms that absorb nutrients from dead matter. Mycorrhizae are fungus-root partnerships that help plants obtain water and minerals. Some fungi are pathogens or produce mycotoxins. People use algae for food, agar, carrageenan and alginate, and fungi for food, fermentation, antibiotics and enzymes. Lichens help colonise bare rock and some fix nitrogen.

sections.heading: Lichen symbiosis
sections.text: A lichen is a stable symbiosis between a fungus, the mycobiont, and a photosynthetic partner, the photobiont. The photobiont is usually a green alga or a cyanobacterium. The fungus supplies shelter and minerals; the photobiont supplies sugars from photosynthesis. The relationship is often called mutualistic, but it can be controlled by the fungus. Lichens are sensitive to air pollution, especially sulphur dioxide, so they are used as bioindicators. They grow slowly and are poor at recovering from disturbance.

keyPoints: Algae are a polyphyletic group of photosynthetic organisms; cyanobacteria are bacteria, not algae.
Fungi are heterotrophs with chitinous walls and absorptive nutrition, growing as yeasts, moulds or mycelial networks.
Fungi reproduce by spores and are major decomposers, mycorrhizal partners and pathogens.
Lichens are symbioses between a fungus (mycobiont) and a green alga or cyanobacterium (photobiont).
Lichens spread by fragments, soredia and isidia and are useful pollution bioindicators.
Algae and fungi have major uses in food, fermentation, antibiotics, gelling agents and agriculture.

en.title: Bryophytes and pteridophytes: life cycles, form and uses
en.short: Life cycles, form, ecology and uses of bryophytes and pteridophytes.

sections.heading: Bryophyte form
sections.text: Bryophytes are mosses, liverworts and hornworts. They lack true vascular tissue, though some mosses have conducting cells. The plant you see is the gametophyte, which is haploid (one set of chromosomes). It may be leafy or thalloid, and it attaches by rhizoids, not true roots. Leaves, where present, are usually one cell thick. The sporophyte is diploid (two sets of chromosomes) and grows from the gametophyte.

sections.heading: Bryophyte life cycle
sections.text: The gametophyte makes eggs in archegonia (flask-shaped organs) and motile sperm in antheridia. Water is needed for the sperm to swim. After fertilisation, the zygote grows into a sporophyte that stays attached and depends on the gametophyte for water and nutrients. The sporophyte makes spores by meiosis in a capsule. Released spores grow into new gametophytes. Sphagnum moss forms peat in acidic, waterlogged bogs where decomposition is slow.

sections.heading: Pteridophyte form and cycle
sections.text: Pteridophytes are ferns and lycophytes. The plant you see is the sporophyte, which is diploid and has true vascular tissue: xylem and phloem. It has true roots, stems and leaves; fern leaves are fronds, with sporangia often in sori (clusters) on the underside. Spores are made by meiosis. A spore grows into a small, free-living gametophyte, often a heart-shaped prothallus in ferns. It makes gametes, and water is again needed for fertilisation. Most ferns are homosporous (one spore type); some lycophytes are heterosporous (two spore types).

sections.heading: Ecology and uses
sections.text: Bryophytes colonise damp, bare surfaces and hold water; Sphagnum peat is used in horticulture and has been used as fuel. Pteridophytes live in forest understoreys, on rocks and as epiphytes. Some ferns are ornamentals; some are weeds. Pteris vittata, the Chinese brake fern, accumulates arsenic and has been used in phytoremediation, cleaning contaminated soil. Some ferns and bracken are toxic, so food use needs expert identification.

keyPoints: Bryophytes have a dominant haploid gametophyte and a dependent diploid sporophyte.
Pteridophytes have a dominant diploid sporophyte and a small, free-living gametophyte.
Both groups need water for motile sperm, so reproduction is tied to damp habitats.
Bryophytes lack true vascular tissue; pteridophytes have xylem and phloem.
Sphagnum peat is used in horticulture and as fuel, and bogs store carbon.
Pteris vittata accumulates arsenic and is used in phytoremediation.

en.title: Gymnosperms and angiosperm diversity
en.short: Major gymnosperm groups, angiosperm families, diversity, identification and uses.

sections.heading: Gymnosperm groups
sections.text: Gymnosperms are seed plants whose ovules are not enclosed in an ovary, so seeds sit exposed, often on cone scales. Groups are cycads, ginkgo, conifers and gnetophytes. Cycads are palm-like with compound leaves and large cones, mostly tropical. Ginkgo has one living species, Ginkgo biloba, with fan-shaped leaves. Conifers are the largest group, with needle-like or scale-like leaves and woody cones; pines and junipers are examples. Gnetophytes include Gnetum, Ephedra and Welwitschia and show flower-like features, but they are not angiosperms.

sections.heading: Angiosperm families
sections.text: Angiosperms are flowering plants with ovules enclosed in an ovary that becomes fruit. Families are recognised by consistent combinations of floral and vegetative characters. Fabaceae (legumes) have pea-like or regular flowers and pods; many fix nitrogen. Poaceae (grasses) usually have hollow stems, narrow leaves and spikelets. Asteraceae have flower heads made of many small florets. Solanaceae include tomato, pepper and potato. Lamiaceae often have square stems, opposite leaves and two-lipped flowers. Brassicaceae usually have four petals in a cross.

sections.heading: Diversity and identification
sections.text: Floral diversity includes symmetry, ovary position, fusion of parts and inflorescence type. Vegetative diversity includes habit, leaf arrangement, venation, stipules and stem form. Identification uses several characters together, not one. A flora, a regional plant guide, and a paired-choice key lead to a family, then a genus and species; pressed specimens and expert help confirm the name. Field notes should record location, date, habit and colour. A plant with square stems, opposite aromatic leaves and two-lipped flowers is likely Lamiaceae, but check the fruit and habitat.

sections.heading: Economic importance
sections.text: Conifers supply softwood timber and paper pulp, and some yield resins. Angiosperms provide most food, fibre, medicines, oils and ornamentals, and much timber. Cereals such as maize, rice and wheat are Poaceae; beans and groundnuts are Fabaceae; potatoes and peppers are Solanaceae. A single family can be useful and harmful: some Solanaceae are food crops, while others are poisonous. Accurate identification matters in agriculture, forestry, pharmacy and conservation, because a misidentified plant may be useless or dangerous.

keyPoints: Gymnosperms have exposed ovules and include cycads, ginkgo, conifers and gnetophytes.
Conifers are the largest gymnosperm group and supply softwood timber and pulp.
Angiosperms enclose ovules in an ovary and are grouped into families by consistent floral and vegetative characters.
Fabaceae, Poaceae, Asteraceae, Solanaceae, Lamiaceae and Brassicaceae are useful example families.
Identification should combine several characters, a regional flora, a paired-choice key and pressed specimens.
Economic importance ranges from food and timber to fibre, medicines, oils and ornamentals, so correct naming matters.

en.title: Advanced plant water relations and mineral nutrition
en.short: Advanced water potential, stomatal control and cavitation, ion uptake, mineral deficiencies and mycorrhizas.

sections.heading: Water potential
sections.text:
Water potential (ψ) is the free energy of water per volume relative to pure water. Pure water at atmospheric pressure has ψ = 0 MPa; water moves from higher to lower ψ. In a cell, ψ = ψs + ψp + ψg. Solute potential ψs is negative; pressure potential ψp is positive in turgid cells and negative in xylem under tension; gravity ψg is usually ignored.

Example: ψs = -0.8 MPa and ψp = 0.3 MPa give ψ = -0.5 MPa. If the surrounding solution is -0.6 MPa, water leaves the cell.

sections.heading: Stomata and cavitation
sections.text:
Guard cells open stomata when blue light activates a proton pump. Potassium ions enter, malate and chloride accumulate, water follows osmotically and turgor rises. Abscisic acid reverses this in drought. Closure limits water loss but also cuts carbon dioxide supply.

In xylem, water is under negative pressure. Cavitation is the abrupt breakage of a water column when air enters, often through pit membranes; the resulting bubble is an embolism. Narrow conduits and pit structures reduce risk.

sections.heading: Ion uptake and minerals
sections.text:
Roots absorb ions. The Casparian strip in the endodermis blocks the apoplastic pathway, forcing ions into the symplast. H+-ATPases create an electrochemical gradient; channels allow passive flux, while carriers use symport or antiport for active uptake.

Essential elements include macronutrients N, P, K, Ca, Mg and S, and micronutrients Fe, Mn, Zn, Cu, B, Mo, Ni and Cl. Mobile N, P, K and Mg deficiencies appear first in older leaves; immobile Ca, Fe and B in young leaves. Nitrogen deficiency causes pale older leaves; iron causes interveinal chlorosis in young leaves.

sections.heading: Mycorrhizal nutrition
sections.text: A mycorrhiza is a mutualistic association between a fungus and a plant root. Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi grow inside root cortical cells and extend hyphae into soil, improving phosphorus uptake; the plant supplies carbohydrates. Ectomycorrhizal fungi form a sheath around roots of many trees and also aid nitrogen and phosphorus capture. Benefits depend on soil fertility and species.

keyPoints: Water potential is ψ = ψs + ψp + ψg, and water moves from higher to lower ψ.
Guard cells open stomata by accumulating K+ and malate, raising turgor; ABA closes them.
Cavitation is air entry that breaks a xylem water column and creates an embolism.
Ion uptake uses H+-ATPase gradients, channels and carriers; the Casparian strip forces symplastic flow.
Mobile nutrients N, P, K and Mg show deficiency in older leaves; immobile Ca, Fe and B in young leaves.
Arbuscular mycorrhizas improve phosphorus uptake in exchange for carbohydrates.

en.title: Photosynthesis, respiration and carbon metabolism
en.short: Light reactions, carbon fixation, C4 and CAM, photorespiration, respiration and carbon partitioning.

sections.heading: Photochemistry
sections.text: The light reactions occur in thylakoid membranes. Photosystem II splits water, releasing O2, and passes electrons through the cytochrome b6f complex to photosystem I. Electron transport pumps protons into the lumen; the proton gradient drives ATP synthase. Photosystem I reduces NADP+ to NADPH. ATP and NADPH power carbon fixation. Oxygenic photosynthesis is 6CO2 + 6H2O → C6H12O6 + 6O2.

sections.heading: Carbon fixation
sections.text: The Calvin-Benson cycle fixes CO2 in the stroma. RuBisCO, the CO2-fixing enzyme, attaches CO2 to ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate, forming two 3-phosphoglycerate molecules. ATP and NADPH reduce these to glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate; most regenerates ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate. C4 plants separate fixation spatially. Phosphoenolpyruvate carboxylase in mesophyll fixes CO2 into a four-carbon acid, decarboxylated in bundle-sheath cells, concentrating CO2 around RuBisCO. CAM plants separate fixation in time: stomata open at night, CO2 stored as malate, decarboxylation by day with stomata closed.

sections.heading: Photorespiration and respiration
sections.text: Photorespiration occurs when RuBisCO fixes O2 instead of CO2. It consumes O2, releases CO2 and uses ATP and NADPH, lowering net carbon gain. It increases at high temperature and low internal CO2. Respiration releases energy from sugars. Glycolysis and the tricarboxylic acid cycle produce NADH and ATP; oxidative phosphorylation in mitochondria makes most ATP. Plant mitochondria also have alternative oxidase, which bypasses proton pumping and releases heat. Net carbon gain is gross photosynthesis minus respiration and photorespiratory losses.

sections.heading: Partitioning and environment
sections.text: Assimilate partitioning moves sucrose from source leaves through phloem to sinks such as roots, fruits and meristems. Sink strength and phloem loading control allocation. Environmental factors control carbon gain: light sets photochemistry; CO2 supply depends on stomatal conductance, a measure of how open the stomata are; temperature affects enzyme rates and photorespiration; water stress closes stomata; nitrogen and phosphorus limit proteins and ATP. Example: gross photosynthesis 20 µmol CO2 m−2 s−1 minus respiration and photorespiration together 3 µmol CO2 m−2 s−1 gives net 17 µmol CO2 m−2 s−1. Over 10 hours, net gain is 17 × 10 × 3600 = 612,000 µmol m−2 = 0.612 mol CO2 m−2.

keyPoints: The light reactions in thylakoids produce ATP and NADPH and release O2 from water.
The Calvin-Benson cycle uses RuBisCO to fix CO2 into 3-phosphoglycerate, then reduces it to sugar.
C4 plants separate initial fixation and the Calvin cycle spatially; CAM plants separate them in time.
Photorespiration uses O2 and releases CO2, lowering net carbon gain, especially at high temperature.
Respiration includes glycolysis, the tricarboxylic acid cycle and oxidative phosphorylation; net carbon gain = gross photosynthesis − respiration − photorespiration.
Assimilate partitioning moves sucrose from source leaves to sinks, controlled by light, CO2, temperature, water and nutrients.

en.title: Plant hormones and development
en.short: Major plant hormones, light control, flowering, dormancy, senescence and movements.

sections.heading: Hormone families
sections.text: Plant hormones are signal molecules made in small amounts, often in one tissue, that travel and alter growth in target cells. Auxin (mainly indole-3-acetic acid) promotes cell elongation, apical dominance and root initiation; cytokinins promote cell division and shoot formation and delay leaf senescence. Gibberellins promote stem elongation, seed germination and fruit growth. Abscisic acid (ABA) closes stomata and maintains seed dormancy. Ethylene is a gas that ripens fruit, promotes leaf and flower abscission and can inhibit elongation. Brassinosteroids, jasmonates, salicylic acid and strigolactones also act in growth, defence and branching. The balance between hormones, not one hormone alone, controls development.

sections.heading: Light and flowering
sections.text: Photomorphogenesis is light-controlled development. Phytochrome detects red and far-red light: red light converts Pr to active Pfr form, and far-red light reverses it. Blue-light receptors control phototropism, stomatal opening and inhibition of stem elongation. Photoperiodism is the response to the length of day or night. Flowering depends on night length, not day length alone. Short-day plants flower when the night is longer than a critical length; long-day plants flower when it is shorter. In Arabidopsis, the protein FT (called florigen) moves in the phloem from leaf to shoot apex and promotes flowering. Vernalization is promotion of flowering by cold. Suppose Ngozi grows a short-day plant near Jos; a street lamp that shortens the dark period can delay flowering.

sections.heading: Dormancy, senescence, movement
sections.text: Dormancy is a resting state that prevents germination or growth at the wrong time. ABA maintains seed dormancy, while gibberellin breaks it; light, cold and after-ripening also matter. Senescence is the programmed ageing of leaves and other organs. Ethylene and ABA promote it, while cytokinins can delay it; nutrients are remobilised to other parts. Movements include tropisms, growth responses to a directional stimulus. In gravitropism, starch-filled statoliths settle in root cells and auxin redistributes, so roots bend downward and shoots upward. Phototropism is bending towards light, caused by lateral auxin movement. Nastic movements, such as the closing of Mimosa leaflets, are non-directional and rapid.

keyPoints: Plant hormones are mobile signals that act at low concentration and often interact rather than act alone.
Auxin, cytokinin and gibberellin mainly promote growth; ABA and ethylene often restrain it or promote ripening, dormancy and senescence.
Phytochrome switches between Pr and Pfr and controls photomorphogenesis; blue-light receptors also sense light.
Photoperiodism depends on night length: short-day plants need long nights and long-day plants need short nights.
Dormancy is maintained by ABA and broken by gibberellin; senescence is promoted by ethylene and ABA and delayed by cytokinins.
Tropisms are directional growth responses, while nastic movements are non-directional.

en.title: Plant genetics and breeding
en.short: Mendelian inheritance, linkage, mutation, polyploidy, quantitative genetics and breeding methods including markers.

sections.heading: Mendelian basis
sections.text:
Mendel’s laws describe inheritance in diploid plants. Each gene has alleles, alternative forms at one locus. A diploid carries two alleles per locus; gametes carry one because homologous chromosomes separate at meiosis (segregation). Genes on different chromosomes assort independently. Dominance affects the phenotype, not the allele’s transmission. A test cross with a homozygous recessive parent reveals a heterozygote’s gametes.

Example: a cross Aa × aa gives half Aa and half aa, a 1:1 ratio.

sections.heading: Linkage and variation
sections.text: Genes close together on one chromosome are linked and tend to be inherited together. Crossing over during meiosis separates them; the recombination frequency measures this. For short distances, one centimorgan (cM) is about 1% recombination. Frequencies near 50% indicate independent assortment. Mutation creates new alleles. Point mutations change DNA bases; chromosome changes alter structure or number. Polyploidy means more than two chromosome sets. Autopolyploids have sets from one species; allopolyploids combine sets from different species. Polyploids are common in plants and can change fertility, size and gene dosage.

sections.heading: Quantitative traits
sections.text:
Many useful traits, such as yield and height, are quantitative: they vary continuously because many genes and the environment act together. Total phenotypic variance (VP) splits into genetic (VG) and environmental (VE) parts: VP = VG + VE. Broad-sense heritability is H² = VG ÷ VP; narrow-sense heritability is h² = VA ÷ VP, where VA is additive genetic variance. Selection response is R = h²S, where S is the selection differential.

Example: if h² = 0.40 and S = 100 kg/ha, R = 0.40 × 100 = 40 kg/ha.

sections.heading: Breeding and markers
sections.text: Breeding combines selection, hybridisation, backcrossing and testing. Pure-line and mass selection suit self-pollinated crops; hybrid varieties use heterosis (hybrid vigour). Backcrossing moves one gene into an adapted variety. Marker-assisted selection (MAS) uses DNA markers linked to a trait to choose plants before the trait is visible. It helps for recessive, late-expressed or hard-to-score traits, but markers must be validated in the breeding population.

keyPoints: Mendel’s law of segregation: a diploid’s two alleles separate at meiosis, so each gamete gets one.
Linked genes lie on one chromosome; for short distances, recombination frequency in percent is about the map distance in centimorgans.
Mutation creates new alleles, and polyploidy is more than two chromosome sets, common in plants.
VP = VG + VE; narrow-sense heritability h² = VA ÷ VP.
Selection response is R = h²S, where S is the selection differential.
Marker-assisted selection uses DNA markers linked to a trait, but the markers need validation in the breeding population.

en.title: Plant molecular biology and biotechnology
en.short: Gene structure, transcription, translation, regulation, tissue culture, transformation, genome editing and GM biosafety.

sections.heading: From gene to protein
sections.text:
A plant gene is a DNA segment with a promoter, a transcribed region and a terminator. The transcribed region includes exons, which are kept in the mature RNA, and introns, which are removed. Regulatory elements such as enhancers help control when and where the gene is read.

In transcription, RNA polymerase II makes a pre-mRNA in the nucleus. The cell caps it, removes introns by splicing and adds a poly(A) tail. In translation, ribosomes read codons on the mRNA, and tRNAs bring matching amino acids to form a polypeptide.

Regulation happens at many levels: transcription factors and chromatin state control transcription; splicing and small RNAs affect RNA; protein modification and turnover affect activity. Hormones and environment feed into these controls.

sections.heading: Tissue culture and transformation
sections.text:
Tissue culture grows plant cells or organs on sterile medium from a small piece of tissue (an explant). The balance of auxin and cytokinin guides callus (a mass of undifferentiated cells), shoots and roots. Micropropagation makes many clonal plants; somaclonal variation (genetic changes that appear during culture) can arise.

Transformation introduces foreign DNA. Agrobacterium tumefaciens transfers T-DNA (transferred DNA) into plant cells; biolistics shoots DNA-coated particles into cells. A selectable marker helps find transformed cells, which are then regenerated into plants.

sections.heading: Genome editing and biosafety
sections.text:
Genome editing changes DNA at chosen sites. CRISPR-Cas9 uses a guide RNA to direct the Cas9 nuclease to a matching sequence, where it cuts DNA. The cell repairs the break, often making a small deletion or insertion that knocks out a gene; a repair template can insert a precise change.

Biosafety is case by case. Risk assessment asks about gene flow to wild relatives, effects on non-target organisms, food and feed safety, and management. Rules differ by country; for example, Nigeria’s National Biosafety Management Agency oversees GM organisms. Check current national rules.

Example: a team in Kenya might edit a banana gene for disease susceptibility, regenerate plants by tissue culture, confirm edits by PCR (polymerase chain reaction) and sequencing, and test only in contained trials before seeking approval.

keyPoints: A plant gene has a promoter, a transcribed region with exons and introns, and a terminator.
Transcription makes pre-mRNA, which is capped, spliced and polyadenylated; translation uses ribosomes and tRNAs to build a polypeptide.
Gene expression is regulated at transcription, RNA processing, small RNAs and protein level, linking hormones and environment to development.
Tissue culture uses sterile medium and an auxin-cytokinin balance to regenerate plants from explants.
Agrobacterium tumefaciens and biolistics are common transformation methods; selectable markers help identify transformed cells.
CRISPR-Cas9 cuts chosen DNA sites; GM biosafety is assessed case by case under national rules.

en.title: Plant ecology: populations, communities and ecosystems
en.short: Population growth and competition, community diversity and succession, and ecosystem energy and nutrient flow.

sections.heading: Population dynamics
sections.text:
A population is a group of one species in one area. Its size changes through births, deaths, immigration and emigration. Unlimited growth follows dN/dt = rN, where r is the per capita growth rate. Logistic growth adds a ceiling: dN/dt = rN(1 − N/K), where K is the carrying capacity, the habitat’s maximum sustainable population.

Competition is intraspecific within a species or interspecific between species. Species with overlapping niches compete; the competitive exclusion principle says two species cannot coexist indefinitely on the same limiting resource. Coexistence needs niche differences or disturbance.

Example: N0 = 200, r = 0.05 per year, t = 10 years, unlimited growth: N = 200 × e^(0.05 × 10) = 200 × 1.6487 ≈ 330 plants.

sections.heading: Communities and succession
sections.text:
A community is all the populations living together in an area. Its structure includes species richness, the number of species, and evenness, how similar their abundances are. Diversity indices combine both; the Shannon index is H = −Σ pi ln pi, where pi is the proportion of individuals in species i.

Succession is directional change in community composition over time. Primary succession starts on bare substrate without soil; secondary succession follows disturbance where soil remains. Pioneer species arrive first, then later species replace them. The traditional climax idea assumes a stable end point, but modern ecology often treats succession as more variable and disturbance-dependent.

sections.heading: Ecosystems and adaptations
sections.text:
An ecosystem is the community plus its physical environment. Energy enters mainly as sunlight through photosynthesis and moves through trophic levels. Transfer is inefficient, often around 10 percent between levels, but this varies widely.

Nutrient cycling reuses matter. Decomposers release nutrients from litter; mycorrhizal fungi help roots take up phosphorus and other nutrients; nitrogen-fixing bacteria convert atmospheric nitrogen into forms plants can use.

Plant adaptations suit their environment. Xerophytes reduce water loss through thick cuticles, sunken stomata or succulence. Hydrophytes have air spaces for buoyancy. Shade plants have large, thin leaves to capture low light.

keyPoints: A population changes through births, deaths, immigration and emigration.
Exponential growth is dN/dt = rN; logistic growth is dN/dt = rN(1 − N/K), with K the carrying capacity.
Competitive exclusion predicts that species cannot coexist indefinitely on the same limiting resource.
Community structure includes species richness and evenness; the Shannon index is H = −Σ pi ln pi.
Primary succession starts without soil, while secondary succession follows disturbance where soil remains.
Energy flow is inefficient, and nutrient cycling depends on decomposers, mycorrhizae and nitrogen fixers.

en.title: Plant pathology and pest management
en.short: Fungal, bacterial, viral and nematode pathogens, disease cycles, diagnosis, IPM and resistance.

sections.heading: Pathogen groups
sections.text: A plant pathogen is an organism that causes disease. Fungi are a major group; examples include Puccinia graminis (wheat stem rust) and Magnaporthe oryzae (rice blast). They spread by spores and often produce visible signs such as rust pustules or mould. Bacteria, such as Ralstonia solanacearum (bacterial wilt), enter through wounds or natural openings and cause wilts, spots and soft rots. Viruses, such as cassava mosaic begomoviruses, are obligate parasites (they multiply only inside a host) spread by vectors such as whitefly, or through sap or infected planting material; they cause mosaic, mottling and stunting. Nematodes are microscopic roundworms; root-knot nematodes (Meloidogyne) feed on roots and cause galls, stunting and yield loss.

sections.heading: Disease cycles and diagnosis
sections.text: A disease cycle describes the stages from inoculum to new inoculum. Inoculum is pathogen material that starts infection. Monocyclic pathogens have one cycle per season; polycyclic pathogens have many, often through secondary spread. Key terms are infection, incubation (time from infection to symptoms) and latent period (time to infectiousness). Symptoms are plant responses, such as necrosis or wilting; signs are the pathogen itself, such as spores or bacterial ooze. Diagnosis uses field symptoms and signs, isolation, Koch’s postulates where possible, and tests such as enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) and polymerase chain reaction (PCR).

sections.heading: IPM and resistance
sections.text: Integrated pest management (IPM) combines cultural, physical, biological, chemical and host-resistance methods. It uses monitoring and thresholds. The economic injury level is the pest density at which the cost of damage equals the cost of control. The economic threshold is the lower density at which control should begin, before the pest reaches the injury level. Host resistance is the plant’s ability to limit pathogen growth. Vertical resistance is controlled by major genes and is race-specific (effective only against some pathogen strains); horizontal resistance is polygenic (controlled by many genes), partial and usually more durable. Resistance must be managed by crop rotation, gene deployment and avoiding continuous monoculture. Case: Ngozi, a cassava farmer in Enugu State, Nigeria, manages cassava mosaic disease with resistant varieties, clean cuttings, roguing (removing diseased plants) and whitefly control.

keyPoints: Fungi, bacteria, viruses and nematodes differ in structure, spread and the symptoms they cause.
A disease cycle links inoculum, infection, incubation, latent period and secondary spread.
Symptoms are plant responses; signs are visible pathogen structures such as spores or ooze.
Diagnosis combines field signs, isolation, Koch’s postulates, ELISA and PCR.
IPM combines cultural, physical, biological, chemical and resistance methods with thresholds.
Vertical resistance is race-specific; horizontal resistance is polygenic and usually more durable.

en.title: Economic botany and ethnobotany
en.short: Plant products, local knowledge, ethnobotanical methods, sustainable use and benefit sharing.

sections.heading: Plant products
sections.text: Economic botany studies plants that people use and trade. Food crops supply energy and protein: cereals such as maize and rice, legumes, roots such as cassava, and fruits. Fibre plants include cotton, jute and sisal; their cells give cloth, rope and sacks. Timber comes from hardwoods and softwoods for building, furniture and pulp. Medicines include quinine from Cinchona bark and artemisinin from Artemisia annua. Oils come from palm, groundnut, olive and coconut; spices include pepper, ginger and cloves. Essential oils are volatile plant extracts used in flavour and fragrance.

sections.heading: Ethnobotanical methods
sections.text: Ethnobotany is the study of relationships between people and plants: knowledge, use, management and meaning. Indigenous knowledge is local, practical and dynamic; it is held by communities, not by one person. Methods include semi-structured interviews, focus groups, participant observation, walks with informants, free listing and ranking. Researchers collect voucher specimens for herbaria so identifications can be checked. Quantitative indices, such as use value and informant consensus factor, compare how widely a plant is used. Ethical work needs prior informed consent, confidentiality and return of results.

sections.heading: Sustainable use and benefit sharing
sections.text: Sustainable use means harvesting no faster than the plant population can regrow. Tools include rotation, quotas, protecting seed trees, cultivating useful species and harvesting non-timber products such as fruit or latex. CITES regulates international trade in listed endangered species. Benefit sharing means communities receive fair returns from their knowledge and plant resources. The Convention on Biological Diversity (1992) and the Nagoya Protocol (2010) set principles; national laws differ, so check current rules. Case: suppose Amina, a farmer in northern Nigeria, shows a researcher a tree used for wound care. With her consent, the team makes a voucher specimen, records the use, and agrees benefits such as training and a community fund.

keyPoints: Economic botany covers food, fibre, timber, medicine, oils and spices.
Ethnobotany studies people-plant relationships using interviews, walks and voucher specimens.
Indigenous knowledge is local, dynamic and community-held; use it with consent and reciprocity.
Sustainable harvest keeps removal below regeneration and may use quotas, rotation or cultivation.
The CBD and Nagoya Protocol guide access and benefit sharing, but national laws vary.
Voucher specimens and herbarium records make ethnobotanical claims verifiable.

en.title: Conservation biology and plant resources
en.short: Threats to plant diversity, extinction risk, in situ and ex situ conservation, seed banks, restoration, CITES and the CBD.

sections.heading: Threats and rarity
sections.text:
Plant diversity is threatened mainly by habitat loss and fragmentation, overharvesting, invasive species, pollution and climate change. Habitat loss usually ranks first: it removes both the plants and the places they need.

Rarity means a small range, few populations, a small population or narrow habitat needs. Rarity is not the same as risk: a naturally rare species may be stable. Risk rises when rarity meets a threat, or when populations are too small or isolated for gene flow.

sections.heading: Extinction risk
sections.text: The IUCN Red List of Threatened Species places each assessed species in a category: Least Concern, Near Threatened, Vulnerable, Endangered, Critically Endangered, Extinct in the Wild or Extinct, with Data Deficient where evidence is poor. Placement uses any one of five criteria: A population reduction, B small geographic range, C small declining population, D very small population, E modelled extinction probability. The list is international guidance, not law.

sections.heading: In situ and ex situ
sections.text:
In situ conservation keeps plants in their habitat: protected areas, community forests, and management of fire and grazing. It conserves whole communities and allows continued evolution, but reserves can be lost.

Ex situ conservation keeps plants outside their habitat: botanic gardens, field genebanks, tissue culture and seed banks. Seed banks are compact and cheap. Orthodox seeds are dried to low moisture, often about 5 per cent, and stored frozen near −18 °C under FAO genebank standards. Recalcitrant seeds such as cocoa die if dried and need cryopreservation or living collections.

sections.heading: Law and restoration
sections.text:
CITES, the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (1973), controls trade through Appendices I, II and III; many Aloe species and Prunus africana are on Appendix II. The Convention on Biological Diversity (1992) asks countries to conserve diversity, use it sustainably and share benefits from genetic resources; its Nagoya Protocol covers access and benefit sharing.

Restoration example: a 5 ha site planted at 1,100 stems per hectare needs 5,500 seedlings. At 80 per cent survival, plant 5,500 ÷ 0.8 = 6,875 seedlings.

keyPoints: Main threats to plant diversity are habitat loss and fragmentation, overharvesting, invasive species, pollution and climate change.
The IUCN Red List runs from Least Concern to Extinct, and a species qualifies under any one of five criteria, A to E.
In situ conservation protects plants in their habitat and allows continued evolution; ex situ conservation holds them outside it.
Seed banks suit orthodox seeds, dried to low moisture and stored frozen; recalcitrant seeds need cryopreservation or living collections.
CITES (1973) regulates international trade through Appendices I to III; the CBD (1992) covers conservation, sustainable use and benefit sharing.
Seedlings to plant = area × target density ÷ expected survival fraction.

en.title: Field botany, research methods and project
en.short: Quadrat and transect sampling, vegetation surveys, plant pressing, data handling and small project reports.

sections.heading: Field sampling
sections.text:
Field botanists sample a small part of a site and infer the whole. A quadrat is a plot of known area, often square, used to count plants or estimate cover. Place quadrats randomly, not where plants look typical: choose coordinates from a map or random numbers. Size and number depend on the vegetation, so do a pilot. Record every species and its cover or count. Frequency is the percentage of quadrats containing a species. Density is individuals per unit area. Cover is the proportion of ground occupied by a species.

Example: ten 1 m × 1 m quadrats in 1 ha held 240 plants of species A. Mean density = 240 ÷ 10 = 24 per m². Estimated population = 24 × 10,000 = 240,000. If A occurred in 6 quadrats, frequency = 6 ÷ 10 × 100 = 60%. This assumes random, representative sampling.

sections.heading: Transects
sections.text: A transect is a line or narrow belt across a habitat. A line transect records plants touching the line; a belt transect places quadrats along it. Transects suit gradients such as distance from water or a path. Keep direction and length fixed, and record position along the line.

sections.heading: Collecting and data
sections.text:
Collect fertile material where possible: flowers, fruits or spores. Note location, date, habitat, collector and number. Press specimens between absorbent paper, change paper regularly, and dry thoroughly so they do not rot. Check whether permits are needed and avoid protected species.

Keep field sheets with unique numbers. Label each specimen with the same number as the field sheet. Copy data to a spreadsheet, check totals and outliers, and back up files. For a small experiment, state a question, use controls, replicate, randomise treatments, and record methods as you go. Report with introduction, methods, results, discussion and references.

keyPoints: Random placement matters more than many quadrats placed in convenient spots.
Density = number counted ÷ sampled area; frequency = quadrats with the species ÷ total quadrats × 100.
Estimate a population by multiplying mean density by the habitat area, if sampling was representative.
Transects are for gradients; quadrats are for area-based estimates.
Press fertile specimens, label them, and keep field notes with unique numbers.
For a project, state the question, replicate and randomise, manage data carefully, and report methods and results clearly.

en.title: Professional practice and ethics in botany
en.short: Herbarium curation, data integrity, permits, benefit sharing, authorship and field safety.

sections.heading: Herbarium curation and data integrity
