sections.text:
A herbarium specimen is a pressed, dried plant mounted with a label. A voucher specimen is the preserved evidence behind a record or study. Curation keeps specimens usable: label each sheet with collector, number, date, locality, habitat and determiner; store it in a dry, pest-proof cabinet; check for insects; record loans; and digitise labels.

Curation also protects data integrity. Data integrity means records are accurate, complete and traceable. Field notes and specimen numbers must match. Never invent a locality or date. Back up digital records and keep the original notebook.

sections.heading: Permits and benefit sharing
sections.text:
Collecting plants often needs permission. A collecting permit allows specified work, sometimes for named species or sites. Export and import permits control movement across borders, and CITES permits are needed for species listed by the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species. Protected areas have their own rules.

Access and benefit sharing (ABS) is the fair sharing of gains from using genetic resources. The Convention on Biological Diversity and the Nagoya Protocol require prior informed consent (PIC) from the provider country or community and mutually agreed terms (MAT). Benefits can include training, shared authorship, fees or royalties.

Case: Amina, a Nigerian final-year student, wants to collect in a protected forest. She asks the forest manager and the national CBD focal point which permits and ABS terms apply before collecting. National rules vary, so check the current official source.

sections.heading: Authorship, plagiarism and field safety
sections.text:
Authorship must reflect substantial intellectual contribution. All authors should approve the text. Gift, ghost or guest authorship is unethical. Plagiarism is presenting another person’s words, data or ideas as your own. Cite sources, quote with marks, and follow the data owner’s conditions. Reusing your own published text without disclosure is self-plagiarism.

Fieldwork needs a risk assessment: list hazards such as heat, vehicles, tools and wild animals, then reduce them. Carry first aid, use protective clothing, work in pairs, tell someone your route and return time, and respect local guides and community consent.

keyPoints: A voucher specimen is preserved evidence and must carry accurate collector, date, locality and determiner data.
Data integrity means records are accurate, complete and traceable; never invent field data.
Collecting, export and import may need permits, including CITES for listed species, and national rules vary so check the official source.
ABS under the CBD and Nagoya Protocol requires prior informed consent and mutually agreed terms.
Authorship needs substantial contribution and approval; plagiarism includes using others’ words, data or ideas without credit.
Fieldwork needs a risk assessment, first aid, a check-in plan and respect for local guides and consent.

en.title: Advanced plant genomics and bioinformatics
en.short: Genome sequencing, assembly, annotation, comparative and functional genomics, transcriptomics, phylogenomics and workflows.

sections.heading: Sequencing and assembly
sections.text: Genome sequencing reads the order of nucleotides in DNA. Short-read platforms give many accurate reads; long-read platforms give fewer, longer reads that span repeats. Plant genomes are often large, repetitive and polyploid, so assembly is hard. Assembly joins reads into contigs (contiguous sequences), then into scaffolds (contigs ordered and joined, sometimes with gaps), using overlap and paired-end information. The goal is a reference genome with chromosomes or pseudomolecules (chromosome-scale sequences). Coverage is the average number of times each base is read: coverage = (number of reads × read length) ÷ genome size. Example: a 100 Mb genome sequenced with 20 million reads of 150 bp gives (20,000,000 × 150) ÷ 100,000,000 = 30×.

sections.heading: Annotation and function
sections.text: Annotation identifies genes, repeats and regulatory regions on the assembly. It combines ab initio (from sequence alone) gene prediction with evidence from RNA-seq and protein homology. Functional genomics asks what genes do. It uses expression data, mutants, transformation and association studies to link genotype to phenotype. Transcriptomics measures RNA abundance, usually by RNA sequencing (RNA-seq): reads are mapped to the genome or assembled into transcripts, then counts are compared between samples to find differentially expressed genes. Careful replication and normalisation are needed.

sections.heading: Comparative and phylogenomics
sections.text: Comparative genomics compares assemblies and annotations across species or cultivars. It finds conserved synteny (gene order), gene family expansion, duplications and structural variation. Phylogenomics uses many genes or whole genomes to infer evolutionary trees. It reduces the error from single-gene trees, but requires orthologue (corresponding gene) identification and models of sequence evolution. Conflicting gene trees can reveal hybridisation or incomplete lineage sorting.

sections.heading: Workflows and example
sections.text: A bioinformatics workflow links tools in a reproducible order: quality control, trimming, alignment or assembly, annotation, variant calling, expression analysis and phylogenetic inference. Record software versions, parameters and reference versions. Example: if a 500 Mb genome needs 40× coverage with 100 bp reads, total bases = 500,000,000 × 40 = 20,000,000,000, so reads needed = 20,000,000,000 ÷ 100 = 200,000,000.

keyPoints: Genome sequencing determines nucleotide order; assembly reconstructs contigs and scaffolds; annotation identifies genes and features.
Coverage = (number of reads × read length) ÷ genome size.
Plant repeats and polyploidy make assembly and annotation difficult; long reads and evidence help.
Transcriptomics uses RNA-seq to measure expression and find differentially expressed genes.
Comparative genomics finds synteny and gene family changes; phylogenomics uses many loci to infer trees.
Reproducible workflows record quality control, parameters, software versions and reference versions.

en.title: Plant biotechnology and genetic engineering
en.short: Advanced tissue culture, transformation, genome editing, GM regulation and applications.

sections.heading: Tissue culture and transformation
sections.text: Advanced tissue culture grows sterile explants (small plant pieces) on defined media with plant hormones. Callus, an undifferentiated cell mass, can form shoots or embryos through organogenesis or somatic embryogenesis. Meristem culture gives virus-free plants; anther culture can produce doubled haploids (plants with two identical chromosome sets); cryopreservation stores lines in liquid nitrogen. Transformation introduces a gene, often via Agrobacterium tumefaciens, a soil bacterium that transfers DNA from a plasmid (small DNA circle) into plant cells. Biolistics (a gene gun) shoots DNA-coated particles into cells. Only cells that regenerate into plants pass the change to seed. Selectable markers and reporters help find transformed cells. Efficiency is low. Example: if 24 regenerated plants from 600 explants are confirmed by PCR (a DNA test), transformation efficiency is 24 ÷ 600 × 100 = 4%.

sections.heading: Genome editing
sections.text: Genome editing makes targeted changes in DNA. CRISPR-Cas9 uses a guide RNA (sgRNA) to direct the Cas9 nuclease (an enzyme that cuts DNA) to a matching sequence, where it cuts both strands. The cell repairs the break by non-homologous end joining, which often causes small insertions or deletions that knock out a gene, or by homology-directed repair if a template is supplied, allowing a precise change. Base editors change single DNA letters without a double-strand break. Off-target edits (changes at unintended sites) must be checked by sequencing. Edited plants may contain no foreign DNA, but regulation differs by country.

sections.heading: Regulation, biosafety, ethics
sections.text: GM crop regulation is mainly national or regional, with international guidance from the Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety. Regulators assess molecular characterisation, toxicity, allergenicity, gene flow and effects on non-target organisms. The European Union and the United States take different approaches; labelling rules vary. Ethical debates include food security, seed patents, corporate control, farmer choice, biodiversity and precaution. Applications include insect-resistant Bt crops (Bt comes from Bacillus thuringiensis), herbicide-tolerant crops, disease resistance, biofortification (raising nutrient content), industrial enzymes, modified oils and plant-made pharmaceuticals. Benefits and risks must be judged case by case.

keyPoints: Advanced tissue culture uses sterile explants, hormones, callus, somatic embryogenesis and cryopreservation to regenerate and store plants.
Agrobacterium-mediated transformation and biolistics deliver DNA, but only regenerated transformed cells pass it to seed.
Transformation efficiency = confirmed transformed plants ÷ explants × 100; for example 24 ÷ 600 × 100 = 4%.
CRISPR-Cas9 uses a guide RNA to cut target DNA; repair by non-homologous end joining usually knocks out a gene, while homology-directed repair can make a precise change.
GM regulation is mainly national or regional and varies; the Cartagena Protocol gives international biosafety guidance.
Applications include Bt insect resistance, herbicide tolerance, biofortification, industrial enzymes and plant-made pharmaceuticals; benefits and risks are judged case by case.

en.title: Advanced plant ecology and climate change
en.short: Plant ecophysiology, phenology, carbon and nutrient cycling, and models of climate impacts on vegetation.

sections.heading: Ecophysiology and ranges
sections.text: Climate change alters the resources and stresses that limit plant performance. Ecophysiology links leaf and whole-plant processes, such as photosynthesis, stomatal conductance and water-use efficiency, to temperature, CO2, water and nutrients. Plants may acclimate through plasticity, but acclimation has limits. A species’ fundamental niche is the climate space where it can persist; its realised niche is narrower because of competition, dispersal and disturbance. Under warming, suitable climate space often moves poleward and upslope, but migration lag, habitat fragmentation and soil conditions can prevent range shifts. Local extinctions are therefore as important as invasions.

sections.heading: Phenology and cycles
sections.text: Phenology is the timing of seasonal events such as budburst, flowering and leaf fall. Many plants track temperature, so warming advances spring events. A simple model uses growing degree days: GDD = Σ max(Tmean − Tbase, 0), summed daily. If Tbase is 5 °C and four daily means are 8, 10, 12 and 7 °C, the contributions are 3, 5, 7 and 2, giving GDD = 17. A threshold of 20 GDD is not reached; three more degree days are needed. Phenology controls carbon uptake and nutrient cycling. Earlier leaf-out can lengthen the growing season, but late frosts and drought can reverse the gain. Litter quality, especially C:N ratio and lignin, governs decomposition and nutrient release; warming usually speeds decomposition, while drier soils slow it.

sections.heading: Models and evidence
sections.text: Climate impact models range from correlative species distribution models, which relate occurrence records to climate, to mechanistic models that simulate photosynthesis, water balance and phenology. Correlative models assume the niche is conserved and can overstate future ranges; mechanistic models need many parameters. Evidence comes from warming and CO2 experiments, long-term phenology records, remote sensing and eddy covariance, which measures ecosystem carbon exchange. Models should be validated against independent data and reported with uncertainty. No single line of evidence is decisive.

keyPoints: Ecophysiology links plant performance to temperature, CO2, water and nutrients; acclimation is plastic but limited.
Fundamental niche is the potential climate space; realised niche is narrowed by competition, dispersal and disturbance.
Growing degree days: GDD = Σ max(Tmean − Tbase, 0), summed over days.
Phenology controls carbon uptake and nutrient cycling; earlier leaf-out can help or be undone by frost and drought.
Litter C:N ratio and lignin affect decomposition and nutrient release; warming and soil moisture modify the rate.
Correlative and mechanistic models, experiments and long-term records each have limits; validate models and report uncertainty.

en.title: Research methods and dissertation writing in botany
en.short: Planning a botany dissertation: literature review, hypothesis, sampling, methods, ethics, data and writing.

sections.heading: Planning and literature
sections.text: A literature review is a critical synthesis of published work, not a list of summaries. Search databases and journals, record search terms and dates, and read primary papers. It should show the gap your question addresses. From the gap, state a testable hypothesis: a clear prediction about variables and expected direction. Define aims, objectives and scope. Check department guidelines early.

sections.heading: Sampling and analysis
sections.text:
Sampling means selecting representative units, such as quadrats, transects or individual plants. Define the population, sampling frame and method. Random sampling reduces bias; stratified sampling may improve precision when the habitat is patchy. Record sample size and missing data. Statistical analysis tests hypotheses and estimates uncertainty.

Example: 20 random quadrats give mean 12.5 plants/m² and standard deviation 3.0. Standard error = 3.0 ÷ √20 = 0.67 plants/m². Approximate 95% confidence interval = 12.5 ± 1.96 × 0.67, i.e. 11.2 to 13.8 plants/m², if assumptions hold.

sections.heading: Field, molecular and ethics
sections.text: Field methods may include vegetation surveys, herbarium vouchers and environmental measurements. Molecular methods may include DNA extraction, PCR and sequencing; use negative controls, replicates and voucher specimens so results can be checked. Research ethics covers honesty, plagiarism, authorship, data integrity and safety. Obtain ethics approval and permits where required; rules vary by country and institution. For work involving local knowledge or communities, seek consent and follow access and benefit-sharing rules.

sections.heading: Data and dissertation
sections.text: Manage data from the start: use clear file names, a data dictionary, regular backups and version control. Keep raw data unchanged and document every step. The dissertation is an argument, not a diary. Follow your department’s structure, commonly introduction, methods, results, discussion and references. Report methods in enough detail for repetition, present results without selective reporting, and discuss limitations and uncertainty. Cite sources accurately and check the final version for plagiarism and formatting.

keyPoints: A literature review synthesises evidence and identifies a gap; it is not a list of summaries.
A hypothesis is a testable prediction, not a general question.
Random sampling reduces bias; standard error = standard deviation ÷ √n.
Approximate 95% confidence interval = mean ± 1.96 × standard error when assumptions hold.
Molecular work needs controls, replicates and vouchers; ethics approval and permits vary by country.
Data management preserves raw data, metadata and versions; the dissertation follows departmental guidelines.
